Putting aside debate over comparisons between Japanese and Western animation and determining whether they are 'similar enough', anime is usually formally defined along the lines of:

"An animated series, produced and aired in Japan, intended for a Japanese audience"

This is slightly more specific than the Oxford definition in order to further distinguish what qualifies as 'Japanese'. I don't have anything against American animation such as Avatar, though anime (being derived from the Japanese animēshon, not the English animation) is typically regarded as something of Japanese origin and is embodied with heavy cultural influences that extend beyond just the animation style.

Something such as Robotech (one of my favorite pieces of American animation) is widely regarded as 'not anime' despite its heavy influence from Macross due to its origin.

What you have to understand is that words don't necessarily have to refer to anything definite in the real world. Much has been lost because humans have trouble with this simple fact. When you learned what an anime is, no one gave you a definition. They just pointed to it and said "That's anime" and you were like "Japanese, big eyes, cute girls. Ok, got it." After watching a bit you also became familiar with common themes and tropes. All of that makes up anime in your mind, and if one or other of those things is missing, it's still anime in your mind just like a three-legged chair is still a chair, even though they might have been defined to you as "four-legged things you sit on."

The important thing is not to get caught up on meaningless semantic distinctions and pose more practical questions. Do I care about watching this? Should this be welcome in this community? You'll find that the answer to those questions will often defy any precise definition. Naruto, Bleach, and One Piece are shunned from some anime communities for much the same reasons as the likes of Avatar. Meanwhile, chan-originated stories may be relevant despite being not Japanese, made primarily for international audiences (that's almost like saying for everyone but Japan), and not have anything to do with the manga visual aesthetic at all.

This kind of semantic hairsplitting happens in a lot of areas. Here's an interesting one: what defines a living being? When you look at a dog and a door, it's easy to tell which is alive and which is not, but what about plants? Single-cell organisms? Viruses? Biologists trying to answer that question (the wrong question), will come up with answers like "growth and death" or "metabolism", but then they miss the major insight: life is not binary, there's not one single point where the inanimate suddenly becomes a living being. A single-cell organism is not alive in the same sense that I am, though we may call both living in a sense. Or what about the original replicator molecules? The ones that gave origin to all higher forms of organisms? They are just molecules that happen to interact in an interesting way. Are they alive? Well, they are more living-like than your average molecule, but less so than bacteria.
